newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy hails ENI success but next sales cause alarm.
newsitem.headline: Italy hails ENI success but next sales cause alarm.

text.p: Italy's sale of shares in state controlled energy giant Ente Nazionale Idrocarburi (ENI) was a record breaking success, but the government faces a bruising battle to get its next wave of privatisations off the ground.

The Treasury raised at least 7.698 trillion lire ($5.1 billion) from the second tranche sale of 14 percent of ENI stock, which closed on Friday, making it the largest single sell-off operation yet carried out in Italy.

Flushed with this triumph, Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi told reporters at the weekend that the government was determined to meet its goal of selling the state's 64 percent stake in telecoms holding Stet by March 1997.
Thereafter, he promised to launch the privatisation of electricity utility Enel, while motorway toll operator Autostrade is also due for a rapid flotation.

Italy's stop-go asset sale programme has been interrupted by four years of constant political upheaval, and although the present government's will to press ahead with its ambitious sell-off plan is undeniable, all three of the above operations are threatened by inter-party feuding.
The most pressing problem is that of Stet.
Italy promised the European Union it would sell the huge group by the end of the year, as part of a deal which allowed the government to rescue a bankrupt state holding company.
However before the sale can go ahead, a regulatory body must be set up to oversee the telecoms sector. Legislation covering this has been stalled in parliament for months.
Brussels has already given Rome a six-month extension on the Stet sale, but the government is increasingly alarmed that even this new timetable might prove impossible.
"There is a hidden agenda," Telecommunications Minister Antonio Maccanico warned last week. "There is much resistance (to the sale) and forces that refuse to come out into the open."
One of the main forces against the privatisation is actually a government supporter -- the hard-left Communist Refoundation which is ideologically opposed to the sell-off.

It has presented nearly 100 amendments to the authority bill and Prime Minister Romano Prodi faces a tough dilemma, working out how he can by-pass Refoundation opposition and at the same time keep his centre-left majority intact.
Some people have suggested the government should focus its energies on the sale of Enel since a watchdog authority for the electricity sector has already been approved.
The trouble is successive governments have failed to agree on a mechanism for the complex sale and Ciampi on Saturday again declined to give a specific date for the Enel sale.
Even a relatively simple privatisation, like that of Autostrade, also now faces a delay after parliament decided to strip legislation concerning its sell-off the from the budget.
The budget bill has to be ratified by the end of the year and no fast track treatment can be offered to a draft law covering the Autostrade sell-off.
"Parliament is giving us grief over the privatisations," a Treasury official said, declining to be named.

Facing parliamentary ambushes over plans to recapitalise and privatise debt-riddled Banco di Napoli, Prodi last week called a confidence motion over the bill, ensuring that the sale of southern Italy's largest bank will kick off next month.
"It is obviously going to be harder to ignore opposition to mega sales like that of Stet," the Treasury official said.
